newsitem.title: FRANCE: INSTANT VIEW - Franco-German EMU pact talks.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Franco-German EMU pact talks.

text.p: Following are comments from financial analysts after Franco-German talks failed on Friday to reach a final accord on a budget deficit control pact that European Union countries hope to agree at an EU summit on Monday and Tuesday in Amsterdam.
IAIN LINDSAY, SENIOR BOND ANALYST, CREDIT LYONNAIS
I don't think there's anything to get overly optimistic about, but you can't say we're in gridlock or that there's been a breakdown in talks.
I would anticipate that if there's going to be an agreement it will depend of a concession by the Germans to the French Socialist party.
They haven't really said anything to sway the market in one way or another. Perhaps the market feels that the spirit for an agreement is there and that there will be agreement.
The general flavour of today's comments has been trying to persuade the general public that things are moving in the right direction.

It's very thin ice the market is skating on. There is a much more serious problem than the rhetoric suggests or than market prices suggest. There was nothing in anything that Strauss-Kahn or Jospin said that suggests that they are going to soften their position. They are sticking to their guns.

The decisive question is still whether the new French government will continue with the financial policies of the old government or not. Given the radical nature of the political change, I think any such continuation can be practically ruled out now. If they did, it would be a complete rupture of their election promises.

My impression is that the mood (at Poitiers) was not very good. When Strauss-Kahn said he hoped that 80 percent of the issues would be resolved by the meeting at Amsterdam, my guess is that the 20 percent remaining is likely to be difficult to be resolved.
I did not have the impression that an important agreement was achieved at Poitiers on the divergences between France and Germany. I also had the impression that Jospin was not ready to bend.

I am skeptical about a formal ratification of the stability pact in Amsterdam. It is not impossible but it is far from being a done deal. (If there is no ratification of the stability pact) at Amsterdam, the reaction will depend on the way it is sold.
